_note: “Did you know?” box on the printable sheet of a word set (src/pages/vocabulary/print/[set].astro): two or three short facts about European Portuguese and life in Portugal, tied to the words of the unit, in the English of the level. Brazilian usage is named as “In Brazil, …”. Machine draft 2026-11-21 (culture run), not yet reviewed by a teacher.
a1-01: Many people in Portugal have several ‘apelidos’ (surnames). Usually the mother's surname comes first and the father's comes last.
Your ‘NIF’ (número de identificação fiscal) is your tax number. You need it for a job, a flat, a phone contract and even on shop receipts.
When you meet someone, say ‘Muito prazer.’ It is the same for men and women.
a1-02: ‘A mulher’ means ‘woman’ and also ‘wife’: ‘a minha mulher’ is ‘my wife’.
In Portugal a girl is ‘uma rapariga’ and a boy is ‘um rapaz’. In Brazil, people say ‘menina’ and ‘menino’, and ‘rapariga’ is an insult there.
‘O bebé’ is written with é in Portugal. In Brazil it is ‘o bebê’.
a1-03: ‘Saudade’ is a famous Portuguese word: a feeling of missing someone or something you love.
‘Estou cansado’ means ‘I am tired’ now. Use ‘estar’ for feelings and states, not ‘ser’.
A woman says ‘Estou cansada’, ‘contente’ stays the same, and ‘feliz’ is the same for men and women.
a1-04: ‘O rés-do-chão’ is the ground floor. In an address, ‘2.º Esq.’ means second floor, door on the left (esquerdo), and ‘Dto.’ means right (direito).
In Portugal a flat is often described by its bedrooms: a ‘T2’ has two bedrooms, a ‘T0’ is a studio.
‘A casa de banho’ is the bathroom. In Brazil, people say ‘o banheiro’.
a1-05: The fridge is ‘o frigorífico’ in Portugal. In Brazil, it is ‘a geladeira’.
‘O duche’ is the shower in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘o chuveiro’.
Many older flats in Portugal have no central heating, so ‘o aquecedor’ (a heater) is a common buy in winter.
a1-06: Breakfast is ‘o pequeno-almoço’ in Portugal. In Brazil, it is ‘o café da manhã’.
In a café, ‘um café’ is a small espresso. In Lisbon many people call it ‘uma bica’, and in Porto ‘um cimbalino’.
Lunch (‘o almoço’) is often the main meal of the day, and many meals start with a ‘sopa’.
a1-07: At the till you often hear ‘Quer contribuinte?’ or ‘Com NIF?’: they ask if you want your tax number on the receipt.
A ‘pastelaria’ sells cakes and coffee, and many people have breakfast there. A ‘padaria’ is a bakery for bread.
There are 100 ‘cêntimos’ in one euro. In Brazil the word is ‘centavos’, for the real.
a1-08: ‘A camisola’ is a jumper in Portugal. In Brazil, ‘camisola’ means a nightdress.
‘As calças’ (trousers) is always plural: ‘As calças são novas.’
Grey is ‘cinzento’ in Portugal. In Brazil, people usually say ‘cinza’.
a1-09: ‘A mão’ ends in -o but is feminine: ‘a mão’, ‘as mãos’.
‘As costas’ (the back) is always plural: ‘Doem-me as costas.’ (My back hurts.)
To say something hurts, use ‘doer’: ‘Dói-me a cabeça.’ (My head hurts.)
a1-10: Your ‘número de utente’ is your number in the public health service (SNS). You get it at the ‘centro de saúde’.
‘A receita’ is a prescription at the doctor's, and also a recipe in the kitchen.
For health advice by phone, there is the SNS 24 line. In an emergency, call 112.
a1-11: In Portugal, ‘tomar o pequeno-almoço’ is to have breakfast and ‘tomar banho’ is to have a shower or a bath.
European Portuguese says ‘Estou a trabalhar’ (I am working). In Brazil, people say ‘Estou trabalhando’.
Many people use the 24-hour clock for times: ‘às 15h00’ is 3 pm.
a1-12: A waiter is ‘o empregado de mesa’ in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘o garçom’.
In Portugal the yearly salary is often paid in 14 parts: 12 months plus holiday pay and Christmas pay.
Doctors and engineers are often called by their title: ‘senhor doutor’, ‘senhora engenheira’.
a1-13: ‘A turma’ is your class group. ‘A aula’ is one lesson.
In Portugal the school year usually starts in September.
‘Português’ is written with a small letter in Portuguese, like all names of languages.
a1-14: Sport is ‘o desporto’ in Portugal. In Brazil, it is ‘o esporte’.
A gym is ‘o ginásio’ in Portugal, not a school. In Brazil, people say ‘a academia’.
Football is very popular in Portugal, and many people support Benfica, Sporting or FC Porto.
a1-15: ‘A junta de freguesia’ is the office of the smallest local area. You go there for an ‘atestado de residência’ (proof of address).
‘A câmara municipal’ is the town council of a município, the bigger local unit.
The post office is ‘os correios’. The national postal company is called CTT.
a1-16: The bus is ‘o autocarro’ and the train is ‘o comboio’ in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘o ônibus’ and ‘o trem’.
Lisbon has ‘elétricos’ (trams), and the number 28 is the most famous one.
‘O passe’ is a monthly travel card for buses, trains and the metro.
a1-17: ‘A serra’ is a mountain range: Serra da Estrela has the highest mountain in mainland Portugal.
Portugal has two groups of islands in the Atlantic: the Açores (Azores) and Madeira.
‘A mala’ can be a suitcase and also a handbag.
a1-18: The weekdays are numbers: ‘segunda-feira’ (Monday), ‘terça-feira’ (Tuesday)… Only ‘sábado’ and ‘domingo’ have names.
‘Dois’ changes for feminine words: ‘dois euros’, but ‘duas horas’.
a1-19: In Portugal ‘o tempo’ means weather and also time.
Summer in the south can be very hot, and the Algarve has many sunny days.
‘O nevoeiro’ (fog) is common on the coast in the morning.
a1-20: The blue, yellow and green recycling bins are called ‘ecopontos’: blue for paper, yellow for plastic and cans, green for glass.
‘O cão’ is a dog in Portugal. In Brazil, people usually say ‘o cachorro’.
‘O rato’ is a mouse or a rat, and also a computer mouse.
a1-21: ‘Ter de’ means ‘must’: ‘Tenho de ir.’ (I have to go.)
‘Há’ means ‘there is’ or ‘there are’: ‘Há um café aqui perto.’
In Portugal object pronouns usually come after the verb: ‘Ajudo-te.’ (I help you.) In Brazil, ‘Te ajudo.’ is normal.
a1-22: When you don't understand, say ‘Não percebi.’ (I didn't get it.) It is very common in Portugal.
‘Ligar’ means to call someone and also to switch something on.
‘Pode repetir, por favor?’ is a polite way to ask someone to say it again.
a1-23: ‘Velho’ is old for things and people, but for people ‘idoso’ or ‘mais velho’ is more polite.
‘Bom’ becomes ‘boa’ for feminine words: ‘bom dia’, but ‘boa noite’.
a1-24: Use ‘a’ for going to a place: ‘Vou ao Porto.’ (a + o = ao).
a1-25: A man says ‘obrigado’ and a woman says ‘obrigada’.
‘Bom dia’ is used until lunch, ‘boa tarde’ in the afternoon and ‘boa noite’ in the evening.
‘Com licença’ means ‘excuse me’ when you pass someone or come into a room.
a1-26: AIMA (Agência para a Integração, Migrações e Asilo) handles residence permits for people from outside the EU.
At many offices you take ‘uma senha’ (a ticket with a number) and wait until your number is called.
The ‘Loja do Cidadão’ is a citizen shop: several public offices in one building.
a2-01: ‘A caução’ is the deposit you pay to the landlord at the start of a rental.
‘O condomínio’ is the building's shared costs and also the owners' association.
a2-02: Owners in a building meet at a ‘reunião de condóminos’ to decide on shared repairs and costs.
Many buildings have a WhatsApp group for the neighbours.
‘Sossegado’ means quiet and calm: ‘Um bairro sossegado.’
a2-03: ‘O esquentador’ is a gas water heater. Many Portuguese flats have one in the kitchen.
A plumber is ‘o canalizador’ in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘o encanador’.
‘Avariado’ means broken, for a machine: ‘O frigorífico está avariado.’
a2-04: People say there are hundreds of ways to cook ‘bacalhau’ (dried salt cod). You soak it in water for a day or more before cooking.
‘O caldo verde’ is a soup with potatoes and thin strips of cabbage, often with a slice of chouriço.
Portugal is a big producer of ‘azeite’ (olive oil), especially in the Alentejo and Trás-os-Montes.
a2-05: ‘O prato do dia’ is the dish of the day, often a good-value lunch.
‘A ementa’ is the menu in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘o cardápio’.
Bread, olives or butter put on the table before the meal are not free. If you don't want them, you can say ‘Não, obrigado.’
a2-06: ‘O médico de família’ is your family doctor at the ‘centro de saúde’.
‘Estar de baixa’ means to be on sick leave.
‘Uma constipação’ is a cold. It does not mean constipation.
a2-07: Pharmacies show a green cross. At night and on Sundays, a ‘farmácia de serviço’ is open: the list is on the door of every pharmacy.
‘O penso’ is a plaster for a small cut. In Brazil, people say ‘o curativo’ or ‘o band-aid’.
Pharmacists in Portugal often give advice for small health problems.
a2-08: ‘O champô’ is shampoo in Portugal. In Brazil, it is ‘o xampu’.
‘O desodorizante’ is the Portugal word. In Brazil, people say ‘o desodorante’.
‘Lavar os dentes’ means to brush your teeth.
a2-09: A CV is ‘o currículo’ (or ‘o CV’). In Portugal it often includes a photo, but this is not required.
‘Despedir’ means to fire someone. ‘Despedir-se’ means to say goodbye.
a2-10: ‘O recibo de vencimento’ is your payslip.
‘O patrão’ is the owner or boss. ‘O chefe’ is the person who leads your team.
‘Fazer horas extra’ means to work overtime.
a2-11: ‘A propina’ is a tuition fee in Portugal, not a tip.
In Portuguese schools, marks in the 2.º and 3.º ciclo go from 1 to 5. Secondary school and university use 0 to 20.
‘Inscrever-se’ means to sign up: ‘Inscrevi-me num curso de português.’
a2-12: ‘O Multibanco’ is the Portuguese cash machine network. You can also pay bills and top up your phone there.
‘Levantar dinheiro’ means to take money out.
MB WAY is a popular app in Portugal for sending money with a phone number.
a2-13: ‘Uma carta registada’ is a registered letter. Official letters often come this way.
At the CTT you take ‘uma senha’ and wait for your number.
A Portuguese postcode has seven digits: 1000-001.
a2-14: ‘O IRS’ is the income tax. Most people submit the yearly declaration online between April and June.
‘O número de contribuinte’ is another name for the NIF (tax number).
‘O prémio’ of an insurance is the amount you pay for it.
a2-15: A mobile phone is ‘o telemóvel’ in Portugal. In Brazil, it is ‘o celular’.
When people answer the phone in Portugal, they often say ‘Estou?’ or ‘Sim?’.
‘Deixar recado’ means to leave a message.
a2-16: ‘O ecrã’ is a screen in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘a tela’.
‘O ficheiro’ is a computer file in Portugal. In Brazil, it is ‘o arquivo’.
‘A palavra-passe’ is a password. In Brazil, people say ‘a senha’.
a2-17: Every shop and restaurant in Portugal must have a ‘livro de reclamações’ (complaints book). There is an online version too.
‘Trocar’ means to exchange something for another item.
a2-18: In Lisbon and Porto you validate your card at the ‘validador’ before you get on.
A return ticket is ‘ida e volta’.
a2-19: Many motorways have tolls (‘portagens’). ‘Via Verde’ is an electronic system that pays them automatically.
Diesel is ‘o gasóleo’ in Portugal. In Brazil, it is ‘o diesel’.
The IMT is the public body for driving licences and vehicles.
a2-20: A ‘pousada’ is a hotel, often in a historic building such as a castle or a monastery.
‘A receção’ is the reception desk. In Brazil it is spelled ‘recepção’.
a2-21: In June the ‘santos populares’ are celebrated: Santo António in Lisbon (13 June) and São João in Porto (24 June).
On Christmas Eve many families eat ‘bacalhau’ with potatoes and cabbage.
A present is ‘uma prenda’ in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘um presente’.
a2-22: A team is ‘uma equipa’ in Portugal. In Brazil, it is ‘um time’ or ‘uma equipe’.
A fan is ‘um adepto’ in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘um torcedor’.
Walking trails (‘percursos pedestres’) are popular, for example in Madeira along the ‘levadas’.
a2-23: Fado is a Portuguese song style, often about longing and ‘saudade’. UNESCO lists it as cultural heritage.
In Portugal most foreign films and series are shown with ‘legendas’ (subtitles), not dubbed.
A film director is ‘o realizador’ in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘o diretor’.
a2-24: ‘O carácter’ is spelled with c in Portugal. In Brazil it is ‘o caráter’.
a2-25: ‘O problema’ ends in -a but is masculine: ‘um problema’, ‘o problema’.
‘Ter saudades de’ means to miss: ‘Tenho saudades da minha família.’
‘Achar’ means ‘to think’ (have an opinion): ‘Acho que sim.’
a2-26: ‘O vidrão’ is the green bin for glass bottles and jars.
Forest fires (‘incêndios’) are a big risk in Portugal in summer.
Do not put plastic bags or used cooking oil in the general bin: there are special points for oil (‘oleão’) and batteries (‘pilhão’).
a2-27: In Portugal the pronoun usually follows the verb: ‘Lembro-me.’ (I remember.) In Brazil, ‘Me lembro.’ is normal.
After ‘não’, the pronoun moves in front: ‘Não me lembro.’
‘Reformar-se’ means to retire. A retired person is ‘reformado’.
a2-28: ‘Faz favor’ is a common way to call a waiter or to say ‘please’ in Portugal.
‘Queria…’ (I would like…) is the polite way to order: ‘Queria um café.’
b1-01: ‘Recibos verdes’ (green receipts) are the invoices of self-employed workers. People use the word for this way of working.
‘O subsídio de férias’ is an extra month's pay for the holidays, usually paid around the summer.
A ‘contrato sem termo’ is a permanent contract; a ‘contrato a termo’ has an end date.
b1-02: The public health service is the SNS (Serviço Nacional de Saúde).
To see a specialist in the SNS you usually need a ‘referenciação’ from your family doctor.
‘A tensão arterial’ is blood pressure in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘a pressão arterial’.
b1-03: Landlords must issue a ‘recibo de renda eletrónico’ for the rent through the Finanças portal.
A ‘fiador’ is a guarantor: a person who pays if the tenant does not.
The ‘certificado energético’ shows how energy-efficient a home is.
b1-04: ‘O título de residência’ is the residence card for non-EU citizens.
‘O registo criminal’ is the criminal record certificate.
‘Deferir’ means to approve a request; ‘indeferir’ means to refuse it.
b1-05: A first university degree is ‘a licenciatura’, usually three years under the Bologna system.
‘Chumbar’ is informal for failing an exam or a school year.
‘O ano letivo’ is the school or university year.
b1-06: People in Portugal often say ‘a luz’ for the electricity bill: ‘a conta da luz’.
Portugal produces a large share of its electricity from renewable energy, mainly water, wind and sun.
‘O contador’ is the meter for electricity, gas or water.
b1-07: A mortgage is ‘o crédito à habitação’ in Portugal.
b1-08: A traffic fine is ‘uma coima’ in Portugal; in everyday speech people also say ‘uma multa’.
A zebra crossing is ‘a passadeira’ in Portugal. In Brazil, it is ‘a faixa de pedestres’.
The rules of the road are in the ‘Código da Estrada’.
b1-09: ‘A manchete’ is the main headline of a newspaper.
b1-10: ‘Discordar de’ means to disagree with: ‘Discordo de ti.’
‘Do meu ponto de vista…’ is a polite way to start an opinion.
b1-11: Many Portuguese towns have an ‘associação’ for sport, music or culture, often called a ‘coletividade’.
‘O convívio’ is a friendly get-together, often with food.
‘Direitos e deveres’ means rights and duties.
b1-12: ‘A testemunha’ is a witness, always feminine: ‘ele é uma testemunha’.
‘Cumprir’ means to keep a rule or a promise: ‘cumprir o contrato’.
b1-13: Many public services are online on the gov.pt portal.
With the ‘Chave Móvel Digital’ you can log in to many public websites with your phone.
b1-14: ‘O sócio’ is a member of a club.
‘O ensaio’ is a rehearsal for a band or a choir.
Many villages have a ‘banda filarmónica’, a local brass band.
b1-15: ‘A greve’ is a strike. Strikes on trains and buses are announced in advance.
‘Fazer escala’ means to have a stopover on a flight.
‘O trajeto’ is the route of a journey.
b1-16: ‘A mercearia’ is a small grocery shop.
‘A peixaria’ is a fish shop. Portugal eats a lot of fish.
‘A bolacha’ is a biscuit in Portugal.
b1-17: ‘Instalar-se’ means to settle in a new place.
‘O costume’ means habit or custom, not a costume.
‘Habituar-se a’ and ‘acostumar-se a’ both mean to get used to.
b1-18: The Portuguese parliament is the ‘Assembleia da República’ in Lisbon.
The President of the Republic is elected directly for five years.
A member of parliament is ‘um deputado’ or ‘uma deputada’.
b1-19: ‘O IVA’ is VAT. The normal rate on the mainland is 23%.
‘O salário mínimo’ is the national minimum wage, set by the government every year.
‘O custo de vida’ is the cost of living.
b1-20: ‘O azulejo’ is a painted ceramic tile. You see them on many Portuguese buildings.
A ‘romaria’ is a religious festival with a procession, music and food.
‘O artesanato’ is handicraft, like pottery and lace.
b1-22: ‘O pulso’ is the wrist and also the pulse.
‘Dobrar’ means to bend, and also to fold.
b1-23: ‘A creche’ is for babies and toddlers; the ‘jardim de infância’ is for children from 3 to 6.
‘O abono de família’ is a monthly child benefit from the Segurança Social.
‘Os avós’ means the grandparents, or grandfathers.
b1-24: If you give your NIF, the invoice (‘fatura com NIF’) appears in the e-Fatura system and can lower your income tax.
‘Os saldos’ are the sales in shops, usually in January and in summer.
Online purchases usually have a 14-day return period in the EU.
b1-25: ‘O largo’ is a small square, often in an old town.
‘A esquadra’ is a police station of the PSP.
b1-26: Portugal is the world's biggest producer of cork, which comes from the ‘sobreiro’ (cork oak).
‘A falésia’ is a cliff. The Algarve coast has many.
The Douro valley is famous for its ‘vinhas’ (vineyards) and Port wine.
b1-27: ‘Um aguaceiro’ is a short, heavy shower of rain.
‘Uma onda de calor’ is a heatwave.
b1-28: European Portuguese often ‘swallows’ unstressed vowels, so ‘telefone’ can sound like ‘tlfon’.
‘O sotaque’ is an accent. The Porto accent is quite different from the Lisbon one.
b1-29: ‘O provador’ is the changing room in a shop.
‘Largo’ means wide or loose, not long. ‘Apertado’ means tight.
‘Experimentar’ means to try on clothes, and also to try.
b1-30: ‘Planear’ is the Portugal spelling. In Brazil it is ‘planejar’.
b1-31: ‘A experiência’ means an experiment and also experience.
‘O investigador’ is a researcher in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘o pesquisador’.
b1-32: ‘O ordenado’ is an everyday word for salary.
Portugal attracts many remote workers, sometimes called ‘nómadas digitais’.
b1-33: ‘Ter alta’ means to be discharged from hospital.
‘O lar’ is a care home for older people (‘lar de idosos’).
b1-34: ‘Os eletrodomésticos’ are household appliances like fridges and washing machines.
‘Avariar’ means to break down: ‘A máquina avariou.’
Many flats in Portugal have little insulation, so heating costs can be high in winter.
b1-35: ‘Submeter’ means to submit a form or an application online.
‘O despacho’ is an official decision or order.
b1-36: ‘O encarregado de educação’ is the parent or guardian responsible for a pupil at school.
‘O ensino secundário’ covers the 10th to the 12th school year.
‘Reprovar’ means to fail a year or an exam.
b1-37: ‘O orçamento’ is a budget, and also a price estimate.
‘Pagar a prestações’ means to pay in instalments.
‘O vencimento’ is a formal word for salary.
b1-38: On a roundabout in Portugal, cars already on the roundabout have priority.
‘O capacete’ is a helmet, required on a motorbike.
b1-40: ‘A discussão’ can mean an argument, not only a discussion.
b1-41: The ‘Banco Alimentar’ is a well-known food bank that collects food in supermarkets.
Many fire brigades in Portugal are ‘bombeiros voluntários’ (volunteer firefighters).
‘Angariar’ means to raise money or collect donations.
b1-42: Portugal has two main police forces: the PSP, mostly in cities, and the GNR, mostly in rural areas.
‘Apresentar queixa’ means to report a crime to the police.
‘O furto’ is theft without violence; ‘o assalto’ is a robbery.
b1-43: ‘A chave de fendas’ is a screwdriver.
‘O berbequim’ is a power drill in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘a furadeira’.
‘A oficina’ is a workshop or a garage for cars, not an office.
b1-45: ‘Seguir em frente’ or ‘sempre em frente’ means go straight on.
‘A seguir a’ means after: ‘a seguir à igreja’.
b1-46: ‘A tasca’ is a small, simple restaurant, often with home cooking.
‘A sobremesa’ is dessert in Portuguese, not after-dinner talk.
You can say ‘Tenho intolerância ao glúten’ to tell the waiter about an intolerance.
b2-01: ‘A chefia’ is the management or the position of a boss.
‘A equipa’ is the Portugal word for a team.
b2-02: ‘A procura’ is demand and ‘a oferta’ is supply.
Portugal's economy relies a lot on tourism and on exports to other EU countries.
b2-03: ‘O incumprimento’ means a breach of contract or a missed payment.
b2-04: ‘O Orçamento do Estado’ is the state budget, voted on every year.
‘Aprovar uma lei’ means to pass a law.
b2-05: Portugal has one of the oldest populations in the EU: ‘o envelhecimento’ is a big topic.
b2-06: Droughts are a growing problem in the south of Portugal.
‘Reduzir as emissões’ means to cut emissions.
b2-07: ‘A burla’ is a fraud or scam.
‘A cópia de segurança’ is a backup.
‘Os dados pessoais’ are personal data, protected by the GDPR (in Portuguese: RGPD).
b2-08: ‘O inquérito’ is a survey, and also an official inquiry.
b2-10: To have a foreign degree recognised you ask for ‘reconhecimento de habilitações’.
b2-12: ‘O stresse’ is the Portugal spelling. In Brazil it is ‘o estresse’.
‘Lidar com’ means to deal with: ‘lidar com o stresse’.
b2-13: ‘Acolher’ means to welcome or take in people.
‘O asilo’ means asylum; ‘o lar de idosos’ is a care home.
b2-14: The Mosteiro dos Jerónimos in Lisbon is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Lisbon has a national museum of the azulejo (‘Museu Nacional do Azulejo’).
‘O património’ is heritage, cultural or natural.
b2-15: ‘O registo’ is register (formal or informal language) in Portugal. In Brazil it is spelled ‘registro’.
‘O tom’ is the tone of a text or a voice.
b2-16: ‘A reabilitação urbana’ is the renovation of old buildings in town centres.
‘A habitação’ is housing, a hot topic in Lisbon and Porto.
‘A licença de obras’ is a building permit.
b2-17: ‘O ordenamento do território’ is land-use planning.
‘A área protegida’ is a protected area. The Peneda-Gerês is Portugal's only national park.
‘O incêndio florestal’ is a forest fire.
b2-18: ‘As ações’ are shares in a company.
‘O juro’ is interest on a loan or savings.
‘O crédito à habitação’ is a mortgage.
b2-19: ‘A rede ferroviária’ is the railway network. Trains in Portugal are run by CP.
Lisbon has two bridges over the Tejo: the 25 de Abril bridge and the Vasco da Gama bridge.
b2-20: ‘O recurso hierárquico’ is an appeal to a higher authority in the same administration.
‘O indeferimento’ is a refusal of a request.
b2-21: ‘A baixa médica’ is sick leave certified by a doctor.
‘O acidente de trabalho’ is a workplace accident.
‘O horário flexível’ means flexible working hours.
b2-22: ‘O prazo de validade’ is the expiry date.
‘O produto biológico’ is an organic product.
‘A colheita’ is the harvest. ‘A vindima’ is the grape harvest.
b2-23: ‘A quota’ is the membership fee of a club.
Big football clubs in Portugal have hundreds of thousands of ‘sócios’ (members).
b2-24: ‘O cuidador informal’ is a family member who cares for a dependent relative.
b2-25: ‘O abandono escolar’ is early school leaving.
‘O apoio educativo’ is extra support at school.
‘As necessidades educativas especiais’ are special educational needs.
b2-26: ‘Chegar a um compromisso’ means to reach a compromise.
b2-29: ‘O parque eólico’ is a wind farm.
‘O fabrico’ is the Portugal word for manufacturing. In Brazil, people say ‘a fabricação’.
‘A central elétrica’ is a power station.
b2-30: A common type of company in Portugal is the ‘sociedade por quotas’ (Lda.).
‘O contabilista’ is an accountant. Many self-employed people have one.
b2-31: ‘Os direitos do utente’ are the patient's rights in the health service.
b2-32: ‘A Proteção Civil’ is the civil protection authority that sends alerts in emergencies.
b2-33: ‘O Estado de direito’ is the rule of law.
‘Fiscalizar’ means to inspect or to check.
b2-34: An IPSS (instituição particular de solidariedade social) is a private social-welfare organisation.
‘O assistente social’ is a social worker.
b2-35: ‘A fuga de cérebros’ is the brain drain.
Many Portuguese people have emigrated, for example to France, Switzerland and the UK.
‘O trabalhador independente’ is a self-employed worker.
b2-36: ‘A cimeira’ is a summit meeting. In Brazil, people say ‘a cúpula’.
Portugal joined the European Union (then the EEC) in 1986.
b2-38: ‘A albufeira’ is a reservoir behind a dam. Alqueva in the Alentejo is one of the largest in Europe.
b2-39: ‘O argumento’ is the script of a film, and also an argument.
‘A banda sonora’ is the soundtrack. In Brazil, people say ‘a trilha sonora’.
b2-40: ‘Criar’ means to bring up children, as well as to create.
Grandparents often help with childcare in Portugal.
b2-41: Northern Portugal has a long textile and shoe industry.
b2-42: IPMA, the weather service, issues colour-coded weather warnings (‘avisos’): yellow, orange and red.
‘A rajada’ is a gust of wind.
b2-43: ‘O percurso’ means a path, and also a career or life story.
b2-44: ‘O ciúme’ is jealousy in a relationship; ‘a inveja’ is envy.
b2-45: In the EU, new products have a legal guarantee (‘garantia’) of at least two years; in Portugal it is three years.
You can complain online with the ‘livro de reclamações eletrónico’.
b2-48: In the EU you may have a right to compensation for long flight delays.
b2-49: ‘O IMI’ is the yearly municipal property tax that homeowners pay.
‘A escritura’ is the deed signed when you buy a property.
‘A humidade’ (damp) is a common problem in older houses.
b2-50: ‘O manuelino’ is a Portuguese style of late Gothic architecture, named after King Manuel I.
The Torre de Belém and the Mosteiro dos Jerónimos are famous examples of manuelino.
‘A fachada’ is the front of a building.
b2-51: ‘As eleições autárquicas’ are the local elections, every four years.
‘O presidente da câmara’ is the mayor.
‘A freguesia’ is the smallest local authority.
b2-52: ‘O avanço’ is an advance or progress.
‘O ceticismo’ is the Portugal spelling since the 1990 agreement (before: cepticismo).
b2-53: ‘A precariedade’ is job insecurity, a common topic in Portugal.
‘O poder de compra’ is purchasing power.
‘O setor’ is the current spelling of ‘sector’ in Portugal.
b2-54: ‘O arguido’ is a person formally suspected in a criminal case.
‘O juiz’ is a judge; ‘a juíza’ is a woman judge.
b2-55: ‘Os resíduos’ is the formal word for waste.
b2-56: ‘A classificação’ is a mark or grade.
Secondary and university marks in Portugal go from 0 to 20.
‘A prova’ is a test or exam.
b2-57: ‘A inteligência artificial’ is often shortened to IA in Portuguese.
b2-58: ‘A rede social’ is a social network.
‘Partilhar’ means to share in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘compartilhar’.
b2-59: ‘A ordem de trabalhos’ is the agenda of a meeting.
‘A ata’ is the minutes of a meeting.
b2-60: Portuguese is an official language in nine countries.
‘A língua materna’ is your mother tongue.
‘O intérprete’ translates speech; ‘o tradutor’ translates texts.
c1-01: ‘Refutar’ means to show an argument is wrong; ‘corroborar’ means to support it with evidence.
c1-02: ‘O orientador’ is the supervisor of a thesis.
‘A dissertação de mestrado’ is a master's dissertation.
c1-03: ‘Designadamente’ and ‘nomeadamente’ mean ‘namely’ or ‘in particular’. They are very common in formal Portuguese texts.
‘Doravante’ means from now on, in formal language.
c1-04: ‘O calão’ is slang or vulgar language in Portugal.
‘O eufemismo’ is a softer way of saying something unpleasant.
c1-05: Portuguese loves diminutives: ‘um cafezinho’, ‘um bocadinho’ (a little bit).
The suffix -ão often makes a word bigger: ‘um carrão’ is a big car.
c1-06: ‘Ater-se a’ means to stick to: ‘ater-se aos factos’.
c1-07: ‘Ficar a ver navios’ (to be left watching ships) means to be left with nothing.
‘Fazer algo em cima do joelho’ means to do something in a hurry and badly.
c1-08: ‘Acarretar’ means to bring with it, as a consequence.
c1-09: ‘A sede’ is the headquarters of a company.
‘Deslocalizar’ means to move production to another country.
c1-10: ‘O défice’ is the Portugal spelling. In Brazil it is ‘o déficit’.
c1-11: ‘A avaliação de desempenho’ is a performance review.
c1-12: A ‘decreto-lei’ is a law made by the government; a ‘lei’ is made by parliament.
c1-13: Portugal's 230 deputies are elected in ‘círculos eleitorais’ (constituencies), using the D'Hondt method.
‘Vetar’ means to veto. The President can veto laws.
c1-14: ‘Absolver’ means to find someone not guilty.
In Portugal a suspect becomes ‘arguido’ in a formal step of the criminal process.
c1-15: ‘Crónico’ is the Portugal spelling. In Brazil it is ‘crônico’.
‘O clínico geral’ is a general practitioner.
c1-16: ‘Ruminar’ means to think about something again and again.
‘A perceção’ is the Portugal spelling. In Brazil it is ‘a percepção’.
c1-17: ‘O sem-abrigo’ is a homeless person in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘o morador de rua’.
c1-19: ‘Desabafar’ means to get something off your chest.
c1-20: José Saramago won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998, the first writer in Portuguese to win it.
c1-21: Portugal has many dams and wind farms for renewable energy.
c1-22: ‘Aceder’ means to access in Portugal. In Brazil, people say ‘acessar’.
‘Digital’ is the same in Portuguese and English.
c1-23: ‘O comunicado’ is a press release or official statement.
c2-01: ‘Pela boca morre o peixe’ (the fish dies by its mouth) means you can get into trouble by talking too much.
‘Quem vê caras não vê corações’ means you can't judge people by their faces.
c2-03: ‘Ténue’ is the Portugal spelling. In Brazil it is ‘tênue’.
c2-04: ‘O bife’ comes from English ‘beef’ but means a steak.
‘O stress’ is common in speech; the dictionary spelling in Portugal is ‘stresse’.
c2-06: ‘Bué’ means a lot or very in informal Portugal Portuguese: ‘bué fixe’. It came into Portuguese through Angola.
‘Fixe’ means cool; ‘giro’ means cute or nice.
c2-07: ‘O alvará’ is an official licence or permit.
c2-08: ‘Os Descobrimentos’ is the Portuguese name for the voyages of the 15th and 16th centuries.
The 25 April 1974 revolution ended the dictatorship of the Estado Novo.
c2-10: ‘Mordaz’ means biting or sharp, about criticism.
‘Vituperar’ is a literary word for insulting or attacking with words.
c2-11: ‘Efémero’ is the Portugal spelling. In Brazil it is ‘efêmero’.
c2-12: ‘Cochichar’ means to whisper to someone, often secrets.
c2-14: ‘A bolsa’ is the stock exchange, and also a bag or a grant.
c2-15: ‘Endémico’ means found only in one place. Madeira and the Azores have many endemic plants.
c2-16: ‘Descriminar’ means to decriminalise; ‘discriminar’ means to discriminate.
‘Iminente’ means about to happen; ‘eminente’ means important or distinguished.
